1023.title: Never again, for anyone
1023.hook: the lesson some draw: guard every people's dignity
1023.howItsDone: Jewish communities speak of never again at Holocaust memorials and in education; some Jewish groups work against antisemitism and for the protection of other peoples facing persecution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line: every one had a name. Whose name did you learn, and say out loud? Today, a vow that grew out of all those names, and how wide it reaches. Day one thousand twenty-three.

Two words. Painted on banners. Spoken at memorials. Typed into arguments at midnight. Never again. Short enough to shout, simple enough for a child to repeat. And the moment you say them, a question opens underneath, quietly. Never again for whom? For Jews? For everyone? For anyone who is next? The two words themselves don't answer it. People do, and they don't all answer the same way. Today, never again.
screen: `TWO WORDS ON A BANNER.` → `NEVER AGAIN FOR WHOM?`

segments.voice: After the Holocaust, never again became a vow. Jews hear it in more than one way. For some, it is first a promise that the Jewish people will never again be left defenseless, with no door open and no one coming. For some, it is first a promise about every people: that no group anywhere will be hunted for who they are. And some hold both at once, and see no contradiction. The second reading reaches back to the Torah's first page. "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him." Not one nation. A human being. The rabbis tell of a debate about the Torah's great principle. Rabbi Akiva named love your neighbor as yourself. Ben Azzai named a verse he called greater still: the one that opens the family record of Adam, the first human, made in the likeness of God. A neighbor can be someone near. That verse takes in every human being. And Leviticus turns the idea into a command for ordinary days: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." Not standing idly by. That's where the vow lives most of the time. Not in grand moments, but in small ones. The persecution this path has traced began small too: rights taken away, words of contempt, shops marked, doors closed. Small steps, each one easy to look away from. So the vow, in practice, is a habit. Noticing the small step. Saying something. Not laughing. Not standing idly by, whoever the neighbor is.
screen: `A VOW AFTER THE HOLOCAUST.` · `FOR US, FOR EVERYONE, OR BOTH.` · `IN THE IMAGE OF GOD.` · `DON'T STAND IDLY BY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to stand against one act of hate. Sit, and breathe. Think back over the past week. Was there a moment when someone was mocked or shut out for who they are? A joke at a table. A comment online. A look on a bus. Don't judge yourself. Just find it. Then picture what one small act of standing up could have looked like: a word, a question, sitting beside that person afterward. Rehearse it calmly, so it's ready next time. If you pray, you can ask for courage. If you don't, hold the scene until the small act feels possible. The bell holds the time.
Never again. A vow made after the Holocaust. Some hear it for the Jewish people, some for every people, and some for both. Today's word.
Your line: never again, for anyone. Today, when you hear a word of contempt about any group, say something, even quietly. Day one thousand twenty-three.

1024.title: Returning to life
1024.hook: after remembering, the tradition turns back toward life
1024.howItsDone: Jewish mourning moves in stages back toward ordinary life; some families end shiva with a walk around the block, and Jews toast l'chaim, to life, at celebrations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line: never again, for anyone. Did you say something, even quietly? Today, the last of these sessions on the Holocaust, and the way the tradition walks back into the day. Day one thousand twenty-four.

The week of mourning is over. In some families, on the last morning of shiva, the mourners stand up from their low chairs, open the front door, and walk around the block together. The neighbors' houses look exactly the same. The mailman is on his round. A dog barks. The mourners are not the same. The walk isn't forgetting. It's a first step back into a street that kept going while they sat. Today, returning to life.
screen: `THE LAST MORNING OF SHIVA.` → `A WALK AROUND THE BLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Torah puts the choice plainly. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses calls heaven and earth to witness and tells the people: "I have set before thee life and death, the blessing and the curse; therefore choose life, that thou mayest live, thou and thy seed." Choose life. It's a command you can't keep once and be done. The tradition builds it into its law and its habits. The Talmud teaches that when a funeral procession and a wedding procession meet at a crossroads, the wedding goes first. The living, beginning something, have the right of way. Saving a life sets aside nearly every other commandment, even Shabbat; the rabbis call this pikuach nefesh. And the toast raised at Jewish tables, at weddings and births and plain Friday nights, is short: l'chaim. To life. Survivors lived this, some without words for it. They married. They had children, and some named them after the people they had lost. They opened shops, planted gardens, danced at weddings. Not because they had moved on. The names came with them. The witness came with them. The questions came with them. But the tradition sets the table again, and pours the wine, and says the blessing, and that too is a way of remembering. These sessions have carried a lot. Tomorrow the story turns to what came after the war.
screen: `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.` · `THE WEDDING GOES FIRST.` · `L'CHAIM: TO LIFE.` · `CARRYING THE NAMES INTO LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one life-giving thing. Sit, breathe, and let these last few sessions settle. Then choose one thing you can do today that gives life: water a plant, cook something warm, call someone you love, walk outside, put on music and let it play. Decide it now. Picture yourself doing it, in detail. If you pray, you can give thanks for life in the words of your own tradition. If you don't, simply notice the breath coming in and going out. That's life too. The bell holds the time.
Returning to life. After remembering, the tradition turns back toward living: choose life, the wedding goes first, l'chaim. Today's word.
Your line: choose life. Today, do your one life-giving thing, and if there's a glass in your hand tonight, say l'chaim. Day one thousand twenty-four.

1025.hook: the State of Israel is declared; for Palestinians the same year is the Nakba, the catastrophe; both memories are real
1025.howItsDone: Israeli Jews mark Yom Ha'atzmaut with celebrations, and some synagogues add festive psalms of praise; it follows Yom HaZikaron, a day of memorial. Palestinians mark the Nakba each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, returning to life, and your line: choose life. What was your one life-giving thing? Today a new part of the story opens, after the war, with one year remembered in two ways. Day one thousand twenty-five.

A hall in Tel Aviv, crowded, hot, with a portrait of Theodor Herzl on the wall. David Ben-Gurion stands and reads a declaration aloud. When he finishes, people outside dance in the streets, and some cry, and some just stand there holding the newspaper. In the same season, in towns and villages across the same land, Palestinian families pack what they can carry, or leave with nothing, and lock their doors behind them. Some of them take the keys. In some families, those keys are still kept. Today's word is the year that holds both scenes.
screen: `A DECLARATION READ ALOUD.` → `DANCING IN THE STREETS.` → `A DOOR LOCKED, A KEY KEPT.`

segments.voice: The declaration that founded the State of Israel is dated in its own text, the fourteenth of May, 1948. It calls the land of Israel the birthplace of the Jewish people. It remembers the Holocaust that had just ended. And it makes promises: equal social and political rights for all the state's inhabitants, whatever their religion, race or sex, and a hand held out in peace to its neighbors. For Jews who had survived, after everything these last sessions have carried, it meant a place where the doors would not be closed. In Israel the day is marked as Yom Ha'atzmaut, Independence Day. Some communities add festive psalms of praise to their prayers. Some Haredi communities do not celebrate it as a religious day. And Israelis mark the day before it as a memorial for those who died in its wars. War came quickly. Armies of neighboring Arab states joined the fighting, and the land was torn through. For Palestinians, this is the Nakba, an Arabic word for catastrophe. Families fled or were driven from their homes, villages were emptied, and the families were not allowed back. Palestinians mark it each year, with keys and names of villages. This path is not the place to settle a war or to weigh one sorrow against another. It is a place to say plainly what people remember. For one people, a homecoming. For another, an uprooting. Both are memories held by real families. Both are real.
screen: `A DECLARATION, DATED IN ITS OWN TEXT.` · `EQUAL RIGHTS, AND A HAND IN PEACE.` · `NAKBA: THE CATASTROPHE.` · `TWO MEMORIES OF ONE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with two memories. Breathe, and let your shoulders drop. Picture two families in the same year. In one home, people are crowded around a radio, laughing and crying at once. In another, a mother turns a key in a lock and walks away with her children. You don't have to choose between them. You don't have to explain either one. Hold them both, one in each hand, for the length of the bell. If you pray, you can pray for both families. If you don't, just let both scenes stay in view, without pushing either one out. The bell holds the time.
1948. The year the State of Israel was declared. For Palestinians, the same year is the Nakba, the catastrophe. Today's word.
Your line: two memories of one year. Today, if this year comes up, listen for the memory you hear less often before you answer. Day one thousand twenty-five.

fork.reveal: on this path, both memories are real. hearing each family's memory comes before any argument.

1026.title: Displaced persons
1026.hook: survivors wait in camps for somewhere to go
1026.howItsDone: Some Jewish families keep photographs and documents from the DP camps where their parents or grandparents waited, and Jewish organizations that once aided DPs still work with refugees today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line: two memories of one year. Did you listen for the memory you hear less often? Today we step back a little in time, to the survivors who were still waiting for a place. Day one thousand twenty-six.

A camp in Germany, after the war. Wooden barracks, sometimes old army buildings, sometimes the same kind of fences. But today there's a wedding in one of the halls. The bride's dress, the story goes, was sewn from parachute silk. Someone has found a fiddle. Someone has baked something that is almost a cake. Outside, the same barracks, the same fence, the same waiting. Inside, people dance. Today's word is the plain official name for the people in that hall.
screen: `A WEDDING IN THE BARRACKS.` → `A DRESS OF PARACHUTE SILK.` → `INSIDE, PEOPLE DANCE.`

segments.voice: The Allies had a bureaucratic term for people the war had torn from home: displaced persons. DPs, for short. Jewish survivors who could not or would not go back ended up in DP camps in Germany, Austria and Italy. Why not just go home? Because home was gone. Families had been murdered. Houses and shops had been taken by others. And in some towns, survivors who returned were met with hostility, and even with violence. So people came back to the camps, or never left them. Meanwhile, other doors opened slowly, when they opened at all. The British, who then ruled Palestine, held Jewish immigration under tight limits, and ships carrying survivors there were stopped at sea. So the survivors waited. And waiting, they lived. They called themselves by a Hebrew name, She'erit Hapletah: the surviving remnant. They opened schools and printed newspapers. They staged plays, held elections, trained to farm. They married, and babies were born in the barracks. The prophet Jeremiah once wrote a letter to exiles in Babylon, people waiting far from home, and told them not to put their lives on hold: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them." Plant gardens, he wrote. Marry. Raise children where you are. The survivors in the camps did something like that. They had a roof, and food, and each other. What they didn't have was a place that was theirs. Nowhere to go is not the same as nothing to do. They built a life in the waiting room.
screen: `DISPLACED PERSONS: DPS.` · `HOME WAS GONE; SHIPS STOPPED AT SEA.` · `THE SURVIVING REMNANT.` · then, large: `BUILD YE HOUSES, AND DWELL IN THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of people with nowhere to go. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind people who are waiting right now for somewhere to go: in camps, at borders, in shelters, sleeping in cars. You don't need to know their names. Picture one ordinary detail. A bag packed and repacked. A child doing homework on a cot. A phone charging in a hallway. Stay with that one detail. If you pray, you can pray for people waiting for a place. If you don't, hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Displaced persons. The official name for people the war tore from home. For Jewish survivors, it meant long waits in camps for somewhere to go. Today's word.
Your line: nowhere to go. Today, give something, time, money or a kind word, to someone who is far from home. Day one thousand twenty-six.

1027.title: Leaving Arab lands
1027.hook: Jewish families leave, or are forced out of, Middle Eastern and North African countries
1027.howItsDone: Mizrahi and Sephardi families often keep the memory of the cities they left through food, liturgical melodies and family stories, and some hold gatherings to record the histories of the cities they left.

segments.voice: Yesterday, displaced persons, and your line: nowhere to go. Survivors waited in camps with no country ready to take them. Did someone with nowhere to go cross your mind? Today, another set of journeys, from cities to the east. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

A black-and-white photograph sits in a frame on a kitchen shelf: a synagogue courtyard, a few men in suits, a boy squinting into the sun. The family who owns it can tell you the city, Baghdad, and the street, and the name of the boy, who is now somebody's grandfather. They can't take you there. Families from Cairo, Aleppo, Tripoli, Fez and Sana'a keep photographs like this, and recipes, and songs. They were Jewish families who lived among Arab and Muslim neighbors for generations. Then, from the years around the founding of Israel onward, they left, or were pushed out. Today, their leaving.
screen: `A PHOTOGRAPH ON A KITCHEN SHELF.` → `A COURTYARD IN BAGHDAD.` → `A CITY THEY CAN'T GO BACK TO.`

segments.voice: Jewish life in these lands was old. Tradition says the Jews of Iraq go back to the exile in Babylon, when the prophet Jeremiah wrote to the captives: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it." Families did that, generation after generation. They were merchants, doctors, musicians, rabbis. There were good years and hard years under different rulers. Then, as the conflict over the land of Israel grew, the ground shifted under them. The details differ from country to country. In some places there were riots and killings. In some, Jews lost their jobs, their property or their citizenship. In some, families slipped out quietly; in others, they were allowed to go only if they left nearly everything behind. Some went to France, Britain or the Americas. Others went to the new State of Israel, arriving with very little. And some Muslim neighbors helped: they hid a family, kept a shop safe, said goodbye in tears. Those stories are told too. Jews from these lands are often called Mizrahi, a Hebrew word meaning eastern. Families kept the old places alive anyway: in Judeo-Arabic songs, in a grandmother's spices, in the way a cousin still says the name of a street in Cairo. Yesterday's line was nowhere to go. Today's adds a piece to the same map: they left too. Saying it takes nothing from anyone else's loss. Two griefs can sit at one table, as two memories of one year did a few days ago.
screen: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · `THE GROUND SHIFTED.` · `EVERY COUNTRY, A DIFFERENT STORY.` · `KEPT ALIVE IN SONGS AND SPICES.` · then, large: `THEY LEFT TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one family's story. Settle, and let your breath slow. If your own family has a story of leaving, from any country, bring it to mind: who packed, what they carried, what stayed behind. If you don't know one, choose someone you could ask, a grandparent, a coworker, a neighbor, and picture asking them, gently, where their family's table used to be. Hold that story the way you'd hold an old photograph, by the edges. The bell holds the time.
Leaving Arab lands. Jewish families who left, or were forced out of, the Middle East and North Africa, carrying their songs and recipes with them. Today's word.
Your line: they left too. Today, pick one Jewish community of the Middle East or North Africa, a single city, and learn one thing about the life it had there. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

1028.title: Many exiles, one people
1028.hook: Moroccan, Iraqi, Yemenite, European and Ethiopian Jews meet in one country
1028.howItsDone: Jews pray for the ingathering of the exiles in a blessing of the weekday Amidah, and in Israel communities from different lands keep their own melodies and customs, such as the Moroccan Mimouna and the Ethiopian Sigd.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Arab lands, and your line: they left too. Did you learn one thing about one city's Jewish life? Today, where some of those journeys met. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

Which tune is the right one for grace after meals? On one street in a small Israeli town, it depends on the window. From one, a Moroccan grandmother's Arabic. From the next, Yiddish. Across the road, a Yemenite family singing grace after meals to a tune the neighbors have never heard. Down the block, in later years, Amharic, from families who came from Ethiopia. Every one of them says the same Hebrew blessings. They don't all sing them the same way. Today: many exiles, meeting in one country.
screen: `ARABIC, YIDDISH, AMHARIC.` → `THE SAME BLESSINGS.` → `SUNG MANY WAYS.`

segments.voice: The prayer book had asked for this for a long time. In the weekday Amidah, the standing prayer, one blessing asks God to sound the great shofar for freedom and gather the exiles from the four corners of the earth. Isaiah had said something close to it: God will gather the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth. The Hebrew name for that hope is kibbutz galuyot, the ingathering of the exiles. Then it began to happen, and it was messier than a prayer. Families arrived from many countries. Some lived for a time in crowded transit camps of tents and huts. Some newcomers from the Middle East and North Africa have said they were looked down on, sent to far-off towns, told their customs were old-fashioned. Ethiopian Jews, who had kept their own long-held ways, met questions about whether they belonged at all. Those wounds are part of the story, and Israelis still argue about them. And yet the tables changed. Moroccan families opened their doors for Mimouna, the night Passover ends, with sweet pancakes for anyone who walked in. Yemenite melodies found their way into popular Israeli songs. The Ethiopian festival of Sigd, a day of longing for Jerusalem, came to be marked by the state. Different chants for the same Torah verses; different foods on the same Shabbat. A psalm says it plainly: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!" Unity there doesn't have to mean sameness. It can mean living side by side, and staying.
screen: `GATHER THE EXILES.` · `MESSIER THAN A PRAYER.` · `MIMOUNA, MELODIES, SIGD.` · `UNITY ISN'T SAMENESS.` · then, large: `HOW GOOD AND HOW PLEASANT.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: taste food from another culture. Settle, and breathe. If there's something near you to eat, a date, a piece of bread, a spoon of honey, eat it slowly and wonder where it traveled from. If not, bring back a dish someone else's family once served you at their table: the smell, the first bite, who was sitting there. Think of the hands that carried that recipe across a border. Later today, if you can, try something you've never eaten. The bell holds the time.
Many exiles. Jews from Morocco, Iraq, Yemen, Europe, Ethiopia and beyond, gathered in one country, each bringing their own ways. Today's word.
Your line: many exiles, one people. Today, ask someone how their family keeps a holiday you share, and listen for one thing they do differently. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

1029.title: Airlifts
1029.hook: Operation Magic Carpet brings Yemenite Jews; Operation Solomon brings Ethiopian Jews
1029.howItsDone: Exodus 19:4, 'I bore you on eagles' wings', is read in synagogue in the Torah portion Yitro, and Yemenite and Ethiopian Jewish families retell the airlifts that brought them to Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many exiles, and your line: many exiles, one people. Did someone tell you how their family keeps a holiday differently? Today, two of the journeys that brought people there, by air. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

An airfield in Aden, heat shimmering off the runway. Families who have come from villages across Yemen sit near a propeller plane with their bundles. Some of them, the story goes, have never stood this close to an airplane. An old man, as it's told, looks up at the silver wings and says the Torah already spoke of this. God bore our ancestors on eagles' wings. He climbs the steps. Today: the airlifts.
screen: `AN AIRFIELD IN ADEN.` → `SILVER WINGS.` → `THE TORAH SPOKE OF THIS.`

segments.voice: The words he meant are in Exodus. At Mount Sinai, before the commandments, God tells Moses to say to the people: "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself." The airlift from Yemen became known around the world as Operation Magic Carpet, and its official name, people say, came straight from that verse: On Wings of Eagles. Years later came another airlift. Operation Solomon carried Ethiopian Jews, the Beta Israel, out of Addis Ababa while a civil war closed in, in a rush of flights, plane after plane. Two airlifts, two very different communities, the same old picture of being carried. Now look closer at the verse. Rashi, the medieval commentator, asks why an eagle. Other birds, he says, carry their young between their feet, because they fear the birds flying above them. The eagle carries its young on its wings, because it fears only the arrow from below, and it would rather the arrow strike itself than its children. So the picture is not just speed. It's a parent's body between the child and the danger. And notice where the verse ends. Not on a map. "Brought you unto Myself." The journey's goal is closeness. This week walked a long road: never again, for anyone; choosing life; two memories of one year; the camps for displaced persons; the families leaving Arab lands; many exiles meeting. Today, the wings that carried some of them home.
screen: `ON EAGLES' WINGS.` · `TWO AIRLIFTS, ONE PICTURE.` · `THE EAGLE TAKES THE ARROW.` · `BROUGHT YOU UNTO MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of one journey. Settle into your seat and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a journey that carried you, or someone you love, somewhere new: a move, a flight, a long drive in the dark. Who carried whom? Who held the tickets, the baby, the bags? Picture that journey from high above, small and brave. If you pray, you can say the words of the verse, on eagles' wings, in thanks for one person who carried you. The bell holds the time.
Airlifts. Operation Magic Carpet and Operation Solomon, which flew Yemenite and Ethiopian Jews to Israel. Today's word, and the last of this week.
Your line: on eagles' wings. Today, carry something for someone, a bag, a chore, a worry, and let them rest for a while. Day one thousand twenty-nine.
